narrative:
The decision to deny your application rests on a prediction that you have a 72.9 percent chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. That means roughly three out of four students with a profile like yours do not pass, and this level of risk is too high for the law school to accept.

The most influential factor in this prediction was your class standing in your third year of study. You were placed in the very bottom decile of your class, while students who were admitted typically sit around the sixth decile. Ranking at the very bottom in your final year strongly pushed the prediction toward failure, because it suggests your academic performance did not improve over time and may even have fallen behind your peers.

The second most important factor was your first-year class standing. Here again, you were in the bottom decile compared with an average near the sixth decile among accepted students. This doubled the concern: early struggles in your program are a strong warning sign for a high-stakes exam later on, and the pattern across both years made the risk even more convincing.

The third factor, your LSAT score of 35, actually worked in your favor. It slightly pushed the prediction toward passing, but accepted students averaged about 37, and this single positive influence could not overcome the two very strong negative signals from your class rankings.

If you plan to reapply, focus on retaking the LSAT and improving your grade trajectory through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. Demonstrating that you can rank near the middle of your class would directly address the two main reasons your application was denied.
